ambitious.meaning: having a strong desire to succeed or achieve something important
ambitious.example: She is ambitious and hopes to become a senior manager within five years.

rebellious.meaning: showing a desire to resist authority or control
rebellious.example: His rebellious attitude often got him into trouble at school.

adventurous.meaning: willing to take risks and try new or exciting things
adventurous.example: They are an adventurous couple who love travelling to remote places.

argumentative.meaning: tending to disagree or start arguments with other people
argumentative.example: He becomes argumentative when he is tired and stressed.

stubborn.meaning: determined not to change your mind or attitude
stubborn.example: She can be very stubborn once she has made a decision.

curious.meaning: eager to know or learn about something
curious.example: Young children are naturally curious about the world around them.

cheerful.meaning: happy and positive in attitude or mood
cheerful.example: She always greets customers with a cheerful smile.

outgoing.meaning: friendly and enjoying the company of other people
outgoing.example: His outgoing personality makes him popular at parties.

sociable.meaning: enjoying the company of other people; friendly
sociable.example: She is very sociable and loves meeting new people.

reliable.meaning: able to be trusted or depended on
reliable.example: We need a reliable colleague who always meets deadlines.

realistic.meaning: accepting things as they are and dealing with them practically
realistic.example: It is important to set realistic goals for the project.

optimistic.meaning: expecting good things to happen or believing things will improve
optimistic.example: Despite the setbacks, she remained optimistic about the future.

pessimistic.meaning: expecting bad things to happen or believing the worst
pessimistic.example: He has a pessimistic view of the economic situation.

generous.meaning: willing to give money, time or help freely
generous.example: She is generous with her time and often volunteers at the shelter.

thoughtful.meaning: showing care and consideration for other people
thoughtful.example: It was thoughtful of him to remember her birthday.

practical.meaning: concerned with real situations and useful results rather than theory
practical.example: We need a practical solution that can be implemented quickly.

musical.meaning: having a natural ability or interest in music
musical.example: She comes from a musical family and plays three instruments.

experienced.meaning: having knowledge or skill from doing something for a long time
experienced.example: The company is looking for an experienced project manager.

relaxed.meaning: feeling calm and free from stress or worry
relaxed.example: After a week by the sea she felt completely relaxed.

identity.meaning: the qualities and beliefs that make a person different from others
identity.example: Moving abroad made her question her cultural identity.

personality.meaning: the combination of characteristics that form a person's character
personality.example: His warm personality makes everyone feel comfortable around him.

influence.meaning: the power to affect how someone develops or behaves
influence.example: Her parents had a strong influence on her career choices.

background.meaning: a person's family, education and experience
background.example: Candidates from different backgrounds are encouraged to apply.

immigrant.meaning: a person who comes to live permanently in a foreign country
immigrant.example: Many immigrants face challenges when settling in a new country.

heritage.meaning: the traditions, achievements and beliefs that are part of a group's history
heritage.example: She is proud of her cultural heritage and shares it with her children.

take up.meaning: to start doing a particular activity or hobby
take up.example: He decided to take up yoga to reduce stress.

settle for.meaning: to accept something even though it is not what you really want
settle for.example: She refuses to settle for a job that does not challenge her.

get in touch.meaning: to contact someone by phone, email or message
get in touch.example: Please get in touch if you have any questions about the course.

grow up.meaning: to develop from a child into an adult
grow up.example: She grew up in a small town but later moved to the city.

first-born.meaning: the oldest child in a family
first-born.example: First-born children are often expected to set a good example.

fun-loving.example: Her fun-loving nature makes her popular with colleagues.

open to.meaning: willing to consider or try new ideas or experiences
open to.example: People who live in cities are often more open to new experiences.

identify with.meaning: to feel that you understand or share the feelings of someone
identify with.example: Many young people identify with the characters in the film.

mixed identity.meaning: a sense of self that combines different cultural or national backgrounds
mixed identity.example: Having a mixed identity can be both enriching and challenging.

cultural heritage.meaning: the traditions and history belonging to a particular culture
cultural heritage.example: Festivals help to keep cultural heritage alive for younger generations.

physical appearance.meaning: the way a person looks, including face, body and clothing
physical appearance.example: Physical appearance should not be the main factor in judging someone.

online persona.meaning: the image of yourself that you create and show on the internet
online persona.example: His online persona is very different from how he behaves in real life.

work experience.meaning: the knowledge and skills gained from doing a job
work experience.example: Employers often look for candidates with relevant work experience.

family influence.meaning: the effect that family members have on a person's character or choices
family influence.example: Family influence played a major role in her decision to study medicine.

suffix.meaning: a letter or group of letters added to the end of a word to change its meaning
suffix.example: Adding the suffix -ful turns the noun hope into the adjective hopeful.

root word.meaning: the basic form of a word before any prefixes or suffixes are added
root word.example: The root word of experienced is experience.

blog post.meaning: an article written and published on a blog or website
blog post.example: She wrote a blog post about her experiences studying abroad.

attitude.meaning: a way of thinking or feeling about someone or something
attitude.example: A positive attitude can help you overcome difficulties at work.

achiever.meaning: a person who is successful in their work or studies
achiever.example: High achievers often set ambitious goals for themselves.

disappointment.meaning: the feeling of being sad because something is not as good as expected
disappointment.example: Failing the exam was a big disappointment for him.

achievement.meaning: something important that you succeed in doing
achievement.example: Winning the competition was her greatest achievement so far.

lifestyle.meaning: the way in which a person or group lives
lifestyle.example: Moving to the countryside completely changed their lifestyle.

nationality.meaning: the status of belonging to a particular nation by birth or naturalisation
nationality.example: She has dual nationality and holds two passports.

survey.meaning: a set of questions asked to a group of people to find out their opinions
survey.example: A recent survey showed that language can influence personality.

climate.meaning: the general weather conditions of a place
climate.example: People living in warmer climates are often described as more outgoing.

mountainous.example: The mountainous region attracts hikers and nature lovers.

weak form.meaning: the unstressed pronunciation of a word in connected speech
weak form.example: Learners often struggle to recognise the weak forms of have and been.

strong form.meaning: the full, stressed pronunciation of a word
strong form.example: The strong form of have is used when the word is emphasised.

blocks.instruction: Read the article. Does it include any of your ideas?

cards.text: Our experiences have a huge impact on our personalities. The jobs we do, the people we meet, our achievements and disappointments all contribute to the kind of person we are. What other factors might also be important?

A lot of people think that our personality is shaped by the size of our family and our position in it. Some argue that first-born children are more likely to be ambitious achievers. Younger children, on the other hand, might be more rebellious and willing to break rules. The youngest child of a family is often fun-loving and adventurous – always keen to try new things. We can inherit personality characteristics, too, like being argumentative or stubborn.

Research suggests that the language we speak influences our personality and the way we think. In a recent survey of international students, Gosia, a Polish-born immigrant in the USA, says that when she speaks English, she feels 'more curious about the world'. Natasha, who speaks several languages, says that she feels more romantic when she's speaking in Portuguese, more cheerful and likely to smile when speaking Italian and more relaxed when speaking in Greek.

Other studies show that where we live or were born might also influence our lifestyle, our personality and the way that we interact with others socially. People living in warmer climates often see themselves as more sociable and outgoing, whilst people from mountainous areas seem to be more open to new experiences.

blocks.instruction: Read the blog post. What do you learn about Sydney's family background, personality and attitude to work?

cards.text: My name is Sydney and I was born in Sacramento, in the USA. My parents are immigrants from China, so I've grown up speaking Mandarin at home but English at school and with my friends. We have family in China so we have always visited regularly. As well as my U.S. identity, I would say that I identify quite strongly with my Asian roots.

In my personal life, I would like to think that I'm quite adventurous. I love trying out new experiences. I'm not particularly good at either, but I'm quite stubborn, so I plan to keep going. I'm also outgoing and sociable.

In my work, I'm very ambitious. I never settle for anything less than the best and always work hard. In terms of my experience, I've been designing websites for over seven years. I co-founded WebDesignSY, an award-winning creative studio. I've designed websites for businesses, charities and individuals. I've also taught several courses in design at the California Institute of Arts and Technology. I love nothing more than thinking of interesting ways to represent you and your brand, so please get in touch.

sections.title: Grammar Bank – Present perfect simple and continuous

rules.label: Focusing on the result of the activity
rules.rule: We use the present perfect simple to focus on the result of a completed activity.
rules.example: He's passed all of his exams. (Focuses on the result – passing the exams)

rules.label: Focusing on the activity itself
rules.rule: We use the present perfect continuous to focus on the activity itself.
rules.example: He's been studying for his exams. (Focuses on the activity of studying)

rules.label: How many? vs. How long?
rules.rule: We use the present perfect simple to answer the questions: ‘How many?’, ‘How much?’ or ‘How far?’ We use the present perfect continuous to answer the question: ‘How long?’ and to emphasise that an action has continued for a long time or is repeated.
rules.example: We've interviewed more than 100 applicants (How many?). We've been waiting for over forty minutes now!

rules.label: Completed vs. unfinished actions
rules.rule: We use the present perfect simple to describe completed actions. We use the present perfect continuous to describe actions that are unfinished or in progress.
rules.example: Oh no, I've missed the bus! (The bus isn't here now, so the action is completed.) I've been learning Mandarin. (I'm still learning, so the action is not completed.)

rules.label: State verbs, experiences and habits
rules.rule: We use the present perfect simple, NOT the present perfect continuous, with state verbs, to talk about states or situations that started in the past and are in progress. We also use the present perfect simple with the words always, ever and never to talk about experiences and habits.
rules.example: How long have you known Jessica? I've owned this car since 2009. He's never driven to work, he always goes by bike.

blocks.instruction: Look at how we can form adjectives from verbs and nouns by using different suffixes, e.g. -ed, -ous, -ful. What is the root word for each of the adjectives in the table? How has the spelling changed?

items.q: -ed: experienced → root: ___; relaxed → root: ___
items.explanation: experienced ← experience; relaxed ← relax.

items.q: -ic: optimistic/pessimistic → root: ___; realistic → root: ___
items.explanation: optimistic ← optimist; realistic ← real.

items.q: -ous: generous → root: ___; ___
items.explanation: generous ← generosity; ambitious ← ambition; adventurous ← adventure.

items.q: -able: reliable → root: ___; ___
items.explanation: reliable ← rely; dependable ← depend.

items.q: -ful: thoughtful → root: ___; cheerful → root: ___; ___
items.explanation: thoughtful ← thought; cheerful ← cheer; helpful ← help; hopeful ← hope.

items.q: -al: practical → root: ___; musical → root: ___
items.explanation: practical ← practice; musical ← music.
